lesson.title: Locating Points of Inflection: The Full Sign-Chart Recipe
lesson.summary: Finding a point of inflection in practice means running the second derivative through the same sign chart procedure used for monotonicity, then reporting it as an actual coordinate pair on the graph, and a single function can easily have more than one.
lesson.body:
The previous section defined what an inflection point is: a location where concavity genuinely switches sign. This section turns that definition into a repeatable procedure for actually finding one, or several, and reporting each one as a point of inflection, meaning a full coordinate pair (c, f(c)) on the graph, not just the input value c by itself. The steps mirror the sign chart procedure already used for monotonicity, only applied to f'' instead of f'. First, compute f''(x). Second, find every x where f''(x) = 0 or f'' is undefined while f stays continuous. Third, use those x-values to cut the domain into pieces and test one point from each piece in f''. Fourth, keep only the x-values where the sign of f'' actually changes from one side to the other, and compute f(c) at each surviving x-value to report the full point.

Consider f(x) = x^4 - 6x^2 + 4. Its second derivative is f''(x) = 12x^2 - 12 = 12(x^2 - 1) = 12(x - 1)(x + 1), which is zero at x = -1 and x = 1, both simple, odd-power zeros, so both are strong candidates. Testing x = -2: f''(-2) = 12(-2 - 1)(-2 + 1) = 12(-3)(-1) = 36, positive. Testing x = 0: f''(0) = 12(0 - 1)(0 + 1) = 12(-1)(1) = -12, negative. Testing x = 2: f''(2) = 12(2 - 1)(2 + 1) = 12(1)(3) = 36, positive. The sign pattern is positive, negative, positive, so f'' genuinely changes sign at both x = -1 and x = 1, confirming two inflection points, not just two zeros of f''.

To report them as points, evaluate f at each surviving x-value: f(-1) = (-1)^4 - 6(-1)^2 + 4 = 1 - 6 + 4 = -1, and f(1) = 1 - 6 + 4 = -1. So the points of inflection are (-1, -1) and (1, -1). The matching y-coordinates are not a coincidence, f(x) = x^4 - 6x^2 + 4 is an even function, symmetric across the y-axis, so its concavity pattern mirrors itself and its two inflection points sit at the same height. This same four-step sign chart procedure works no matter how many candidates a function produces, and reporting the coordinate pair rather than just the x-value keeps the point of inflection tied to an actual, plottable location on the curve.
